item.title: How to Resist Overthinking Decisions
item.description:
Decision-Making

How to Resist Overthinking Decisions

You can’t control the future. But you can decide well and feel better about it.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Thinking more by slowing decisions and reviewing more data can lead to better decisions.
  • However, overthinking occurs when we get stuck in a loop and can't move forward.
  • You can learn how to avoid a repetitive loop that feels unpleasant and does not improve decision quality.

Scientifically, overthinking is not a singular phenomenon. But because the experience is common to many people, we use an umbrella term to describe different mental patterns. In this post, you’ll learn to spot typical patterns you may fall into, and how you can not only resist those patterns but also make better decisions and feel more confident in them.

But thinking more usually improves decisions!

Much of the scientific literature on decision-making recommends taking more time and reviewing more data. When advising leaders, social scientists and business scholars alike recommend practices that slow the decision process and force a wider range of evidence to be considered [1,2]. In my own work developing people’s leadership, communication and influencing skills, my goal is to instill a pause before your automatic response, so you can respond in a manner that is more effective than your usual, default approach.

But thinking longer does not always improve outcomes and can cause emotional distress. So, when does thinking become overthinking: a repetitive loop that feels unpleasant and does not improve decision quality?

Overthinking is a common experience
Source: AI Image: ChatGPT / OpenAI

When we prolong the decision without improving it

Neuroscientists have proposed that our brains treat the effort of evaluating different options as a cost we pay in order to buy confidence [3]. As a result, we stop thinking once we feel confident enough. However, if you can’t reach the point of feeling confident enough – because you can’t verify the value of the options or distinguish between them – you may keep reviewing the same evidence. Your brain keeps “paying” in time and effort without gaining any reassurance.

Postponing the decision may itself dwindle your confidence. Computational modelling indicates that we use our decision-making time as a direct source of information about our confidence in that decision [4]. Thus, the longer we take to decide, the less confident and more uncomfortable we may feel, particularly when there is no new information available.

What form of overthinking do you experience?

Here are three common variants you might recognise in yourself:

  1. Maximising: When you aim for the optimal outcome every time. People who exhaustively seek out the best possible option are generally less happy. Although maximisers may even achieve better outcomes, their arduous decision process is so psychologically taxing that it lowers satisfaction and increases stress. As a result, they tend to be less optimistic, more neurotic, and more likely to ruminate over past decisions [5].
  2. Choice overload: When it's impossible to choose between options. The stress of choice overload is not simply a function of the number of options available. It comes from the difficulty of distinguishing between those options and assessing how attractive they are. The more you care about the outcome, the worse it feels [6].
  3. Rumination: Focusing on your feelings instead of the problem. When struggling with a decision you might feel anxious or worried. You can do one of two things: 1) reflect on the situation to move forward, or 2) focus on the feeling. Rumination is the latter: a repetitive pattern of focus on the negative emotion, which is likely to worsen your mood [7] and can even lead to depression [8]. Rumination is more common in women but occurs in both genders, particularly in young to mid-adulthood [9].

How to resist the overthinking pattern and improve your decision process

A few simple but powerful steps can help a great deal.

  • Recognise that you cannot fully control the future. An optimal decision using the best available evidence still cannot account for everything that might affect the outcome. This is hard to recognise because in hindsight we equate decision outcome with decision quality – but excellent decisions can bring bad results, and poor decisions sometimes lead to great outcomes. Factors we don’t control (context, timing, others’ choices) have a bigger role than we give them credit for. You cannot control the outcome; you can only control the decision.
  • Control your maximising tendency by re-focusing it. A metanalysis of more than 47,000 people found that well-being is not negatively affected when maximisers aim to achieve the best decision process. The negative effects occur when the maximiser’s goal is the best outcome [10]. Unsurprisingly, the analysis found the highest reductions in well-being for maximisers focused on their careers and relationships, where outcomes always depend on factors we don’t control.
  • Reduce choice overload by naming what matters most. Whether you are choosing between holiday locations or new career opportunities, your options rarely permit an apples-to-apples comparison. However, a significant factor in choice overload is uncertainty about the goal [6]. When you can’t determine which option is clearly the best, define your goal better. For example, if you can’t choose between Cancun, Casablanca, or Cape Town, first clarify your top goal for your week away, then evaluate which option fits it best. Choosing one thing always means choosing to not have other things. Accept your decision as the best you could do at the time.
  • Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) techniques can break the rumination loop. CBT is a well-established approach that changes your thoughts in order to change your mood and your actions. CBT researchers treat rumination as a learned response that can be interrupted by shifting your focus from why you feel this way to how you can address the situation [11]. Your overthinking might include “why” themes such as, “Why am I no good at making decisions? Why do I always second-guess myself?” Break the rumination cycle by shifting to, “How can I make the best decision today? What is the first step?”.
  • Reduce your fear of getting it wrong. CBT also enables people to reduce their worries about the future. The technique is called “de-catastrophising,” and the simplest version involves three steps:
    • State the worst outcome in concrete detail: What happens, to whom and when.
    • Estimate the percentage likelihood of this outcome (between 0% and 100%).
    • State how you could cope if the worst case actually occurred.

A field study found that it’s rare your worst fear comes true, but even if it does, you will likely cope better than you expected [12].

Many of our personal challenges are common patterns in human behaviour. They become easier to manage when we understand why they happen, and what has been shown to help.

item.title: 5 Awesome Strategies to Strengthen Your Love of Learning
item.description:
Education

5 Awesome Strategies to Strengthen Your Love of Learning

Why a love of learning is so beneficial and how you can improve it.

Posted August 3, 2026

Source: Oleksandr Pidvalny / Pixabay

Whatever your age—childhood, teen years, or adulthood—in each season of life, love of learning offers a powerful engine for coping, thriving, and living a life well lived. Learning can be beneficial at any age and stage of the life span. And curiosity, a natural motivator and teacher from early childhood and forward, is sparked and nurtured through relationships, asking questions, and noting the responses of others (Hau, 2026).

Love of learning is one of the 24 character strengths common to humankind, and “it reflects a passion for learning new ideas, skills, or information, not for external rewards but for the personal satisfaction it brings" (VIA.org, 2026). For some of us, love of learning is a signature character strength that supports a deeper desire and interest in learning.

Research conducted by Umuco et al. (2022) studied over 11,000 people with emotional, physical, and cognitive disabilities and examined their character strengths. The researchers found that among most people with disabilities that they studied, love of learning was in the top five strengths and can help people thrive.

Some years ago, my father told me a story about how he expanded his parenting skills. He described reading articles in Readers Digest magazine when he was a middle-aged parent, and I was a child. My dad explained that parenting was not something he felt like he knew a lot about, so to learn more he would study articles in magazines and newspapers (Berns-Zare, 2025). Recalling this conversation is a poignant reminder about the value of learning throughout our lifespan.

There are many reasons why learning is important, from basic literacy and life skills to academic and job performance, to productivity and living with meaning and purpose.

In each decade of our lives and in our interactions with others, it can be helpful to have a good understanding of what love of learning actually is, so we are able to notice it in ourselves and in others (APA, 2026; VIA.org, 2026). For example, a parent, grandparent, or teacher recognizing the love of learning in a child or adolescent as they learn a new skill or read a book they enjoy, or a friend noticing another friend’s great pleasure as they learn in a class together.

There are many ways to nurture love of learning and boost your own ability to thrive. Here are 5 strategies (Berns-Zare, 2025):

  1. Listening actively in the conversations of daily life. Much can be learned via relationships – with children, peers, co-workers, elders, the person sitting next to you on the plane or in the checkout line at the store.
  2. Taking advantage of a variety of learning opportunities, such as listening to webinars and podcasts, reading fiction or nonfiction, taking a class at the library or online.
  3. Trying new activities. Consider what you want to learn about or what you would benefit from learning more about in the course of your daily life and work.
  4. Pausing to consider and collect nuggets of wisdom from your observations and experiences. For example: what can you learn from a setback to turn it into a growth experience or opportunity?
  5. Nurturing a growth mindset (Dweck, 2016). People with a growth mindset believe that with effort and experience, we have the capacity to learn, improve, and perform better in education, life, and work.

How can you strengthen learning in your life?

item.title: What Is the World Asking of You?
item.description:
Anxiety

What Is the World Asking of You?

You were made for this time of uncertainty; you’re needed more than ever before.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • The first step in working with uncertainty is: Accept discomfort.
  • Second step: Become curious and explore your uncertainty.
  • Mindfulness, researchers have found, can help regulate aversive reactions to uncertainty.
Source: istock/Iryna Martynenko

During times of uncertainty, it’s natural to experience a range of emotions, heightened levels of stress, and even confusion, as well as mood changes, among other reactions. Of course, the extraordinary and dire circumstances of living in the middle of a war, security threats, or occupation requires a vigilance around uncertainty that is quite different from living in a place where there’s relative safety and order.

When you arrive at a place that feels like you just can’t go on, this is the time to pause. Allow this to sink in. Acknowledging this is the beginning of moving into a state of greater inner freedom and resolve.

Hidden Messages in Times of Crisis

What if the current challenges in the world are just what you need right now to grow and flourish? What if times of crisis can serve as a kind of active agent, a lever that inspires personal and collective change? What if these circumstances which present themselves as unsettling and uncomfortable will soon grow into stronger and more robust qualities of leadership?

First step: Accept discomfort. Mindfulness practices and meditation can help.

Second step: Become curious and explore your uncertainty.

While many of us are conditioned to "buck up" and "get strong" in the face of stress or as activists working on an important cause, it’s helpful to explore your authentic response to uncertainty. What does living through a phase of the unknown trigger in you?

Uncertainty and Future Threats

It’s not surprising that researchers have found that uncertainty about future threats can lead to increased anxiety. It’s theorized that five processes are involved in poor responses to future threats: inflated estimates of threat cost and probability, hypervigilance, deficient safety learning, behavioral and cognitive avoidance, and heightened reactivity to threat uncertainty.

Mindfulness, researchers have found, can help regulate aversive reactions to uncertainty. The practice can help alter perceptions of uncertainty as “unacceptable” or needing to be stopped.

Once there’s more comfort with uncertainty, new possibilities can arise — which may include positive benefits.

Five Categories of Not Knowing

In his chapter "Not Knowing" of the book Uncertainty: A Catalyst for Creativity, Learning and Development, Vlad P. Glăveanu organizes categories of not knowing into the following possible states: certain knowledge and the experience of trust; uncertain not knowing and the experience of anxiety; uncertain knowing and the experience of curiosity; and certain not knowing and the experience of wonder. Biologists will recognize a similar use of these terms in DNA barcoding.

Think of “certain knowledge” as the foundation of education — multiplication, grammar rules, and biology. “Uncertain not knowing”, according to the author, is “a state in which we don't only miss a clear understanding of things, but we are also uncertain about what exactly it is that we don’t know. It is an unsettling experience that many individuals try to avoid on a daily basis.” Psychologists and others who study uncertainty can utilize the intolerance of uncertainty scale as a measurement tool for this.

It’s clearly impossible to live with uncertainty for indefinite periods. But even for short periods, some people find they are more reactive than others to “uncertain not knowing,” which leads to defenses, including ignoring or trivializing uncertainty, or attempting to eliminate uncertainty by coming up with explanations.

“Another way is to contain this kind of anxiety and focus on what we do know or are certain about as a way of moving forward and continuing to act decisively,” notes Glăveanu. When we become aware of this liminal state between knowing and uncertainty and embrace it, we begin to open to all possibilities, the space where creativity and fresh insights can blossom.

“Uncertain knowing” opens up the possibility of curiosity — the reflection that is inquisitive and probing, with no end goal in mind. And this last state, “Certain not knowing”, takes this one step deeper into what we might call the open space of the mystical or spiritual realms. Here the author brings in wonder, and says that “building knowledge commits us to a given reading of reality, one that makes other readings unlikely or labels them as wrong. Not knowing, on the contrary, excludes singular constructions of the world and, as such, escapes easy, dominant or hegemonic ones. In recognizing one’s lack of knowledge rests the humility to learn from various perspectives and to still question each of them, in turn.”

Uncertainty as a Practice

We are used to practices related to action, discipline, and movement. But what if during a time of rapid change, we turn towards being, not doing? What does it mean to simply be without an action step?

If we are witnessing a world that is full of unknowns and uncertainties — and one that is possibly hitting a dead end — is that okay? Maybe as humanity we have come to a point that we don’t know. Instead of rejecting this, we could work with this reality — maybe it’s part of the architecture of this moment not to know.

The old ways of living and function may be expiring; some of the new ways don’t yet belong, and haven’t yet entered our collective awareness. The skill is to learn how to dwell in uncertainty, dwell in not knowing, dwell in liminal space, the in-between.

Sometimes life shows us a clear path. If that’s the case, then the direction is straightforward. Sometimes it’s easy to find out information, but sometimes the direction points to a new development that needs space to arise and make itself known. If I judge myself for not knowing, I don’t give myself that space. I get stuck.

When should I give myself space? Whenever I face an uncertain situation, I can respond to it by saying honestly, “I really don’t know how to relate to this.” Let’s have that instead of struggling with it.

Next, see what happens when we ask ourselves, “What’s in there?” “What does life show me here?” “What happens when I slow down and ask, what’s the higher choice? What serves more?”

Sometimes the answer is not in the doing; it’s in the being that allows another answer to arise, another level of insight. This practice is not the only solution during this time but it is part of the solution. Listen to the space that is pregnant with the next level of development.

Creative Learning on the Path to Healing

As Glăveanu writes, “Creative learning itself can be defined as a fluid movement between certainty and uncertainty, knowing and not knowing that requires, at every stage, a between anxiety, trust, curiosity and wonder.”

Part of the healing process is that we don’t know who we will become. When we’re on an active path of transformation, there’s not a way back to a healed state, but only a way forward into a new future and a new life we don’t yet know. It reveals itself in the change process, once that next step is taken.

We don’t know where the path will lead; but still, we are following the path. That’s what matters. The unknown then becomes a catalyst for something new to enter.

item.title: Can Utilitarianism Replace Ethics?
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Can Utilitarianism Replace Ethics?

Do we still need moral philosophers?

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Utilitarianism is seen as the most pragmatic tool for resolving conflicting subjective values.
  • Utilitarianism offers transparency in moral trade-offs, unlike theories claiming objective truths.
  • Embracing moral nihilism could render traditional moral philosophy largely obsolete.

This is a continuation from a previous blog post on the future of moral philosoph (see here).

In his PhD thesis, the psychologist Jushua Greene wrote:

Utilitarianism is not true, nor is it an adequate systematization of anyone’s values. No one is a utilitarian at heart. But at the same time, everyone is a utilitarian in part. As realists, relying on our moral intuitions as guides to moral truth, we have every reason to reject utilitarianism. But as people who know the truth about morality in search of practical moral guidelines that people with different moral outlooks can share, utilitarianism is, I think, our best hope.

Utilitarianism is unattractive to many because it involves trade-offs and compromises. The real ethical truths could not possibly be so cruel. But there are no moral facts. There is only the harsh real world of millions of beings, many more if we include animals, who all have their own subjective values, which will inevitably come into conflict with one another.

To deal with these situations, there is no better tool than utilitarianism, for it makes those trade-offs explicit and transparent, whereas other ethical theories offer little more than the dictatorship of allegedly objective values, with a propaganda minister who declares any criticism or mention of trade-offs immoral.

And, of course, yes. Yes, of course…

The answers offered by a utilitarian approach to social problems will be unsatisfying in the same way that planning a holiday among a group of friends with very different visions of the ideal holiday will be. One wants to go skiing. One wants to be at the beach. One wants to rest a lot. Another wants to party. Imagine if one of these friends came up with an objective theory of holidaying, defending the one true way by which different holidays could be assessed, one that just so happens to coincide with their own preferred destination.

That is how moral discourse looks to the moral nihilist.

I hate to break it to you, but scaling these problems up to millions of individuals makes them even harder. None of the objections to utilitarianism as the one true and final theory of ethics carries much weight against utilitarianism as an inevitable pragmatic tool. Nothing else can do better. Any deviation reduces the amount of (subjective) value in the world.

J. L. Mackie, the father of moral error theory, advocated a kind of moral revisionism that cleansed ethics of its problematic parts and left it with a kind of pragmatic remainder that came pretty close to utilitarianism. In his own words:

No doubt my approach could be called, in a very broad sense, a rule utilitarian one

And Bentham and Mill, the founders of utilitarianism, might have seen the need to combine moral nihilism with utilitarianism as well. They were ultimately social reformers, engaged in law and governance, as much as they were part-time philosophers. The 18th and 19th century was no time to advocate for moral nihilism to promote social coordination and welfare. A utilitarian, after all, might well lie about their views on meta-ethics if they believe that this would make more people into utilitarians.

Reflections from my recent pilgrimage to the father of utilitarianism

Bentham once wrote in his An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation:

When thus interpreted [in light of the principle of utility], the words ought, and right and wrong, and others of that stamp, have a meaning: when otherwise, they have none.

He does not believe that these moral terms are even intelligible, unless they are translated in terms of utility. I read this as an endorsement of moral nihilism, with an appeal to rewrite our moral terms, by casting all previous thinking, so harmful to human and animal flourishing, into the flames.

Moral nihilism, in the end, is the liberation of values. The only real values there are: subjective ones. Even a traditional objectivist utilitarian could instrumentally endorse moral nihilism, for it would free us from the many harms that moral zealotry causes today. But I ultimately endorse utilitarianism as the best pragmatic tool for all of us, including other animals, to realise our values in a world where they will inevitably clash with one another. That this would be an amoral society is no objection. For we would all be better off if we cast off the yoke of tyranny that is morality.

But now it seems that there is no work left to be done for moral philosophers. Meta-ethics is abolished once we adopt moral nihilism and normative ethics is fully replaced to the empirical study of how we can optimally resolve our conflicts. If so, that would be wonderful. A sign of a mature field that has actually made progress in offering us guidance for how to act.

Of course, this is the very reason so many moral philosophers despise nihilism and utilitarianism. Not because these views are false. But because they rightly believe that this would mean that their job here is done and that they’ve wasted much of their lifetime defending theories that aren’t even close to truth.

And so they desperatedly cling to their alternatives, much like the vast majority of religious leaders are never seriously going to question their religious beliefs — incentivized to keep believing in a myth.

But just as philosophers of science aren’t obsolete in modern science, moral philosophers are given a new role to play — that is, as philosophers of ‘moral’ science. A role that is admittedly quite different from much of what goes on in the offices of moral philosophers.

item.title: Why Don't Talented People Get Promoted More Often?
item.description:
Leadership

Why Don't Talented People Get Promoted More Often?

The hidden cost of always being the person everyone depends on.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Being the constant fixer builds reliability, but doesn't make you promotable.
  • Before saying yes, ask if this is the best use of your expertise.
  • Create future leaders and systems, not dependence on you and your expertise.
  • Your goal isn't to be indispensable. It's to be seen as promotable.
What do people value more, your leadership or labor?
Source: Vitaly Gabriel/Unsplash

It’s promotion season. Everyone smiles and congratulates the person who got promoted. Yet, some people are thinking something else entirely. They are thankful you didn’t get promoted because they desperately need you right where you are. But you are beginning to realize what they value is not your leadership. What they rely on is your labor.

This is the Competency Tax (read my Psychology Today piece about it here), the hidden cost of being dependable. The good news is that it doesn’t need to be an endless loop of despair. There are immediate steps you can take to break the cycle and start being seen as undeniable for the next promotion.

So why does this continuously happen to high performers (read more about that here)? Perhaps there is part of their identity which is formed from continuously being the person others depend on. At least initially, helping others feels rewarding and being trusted feels validating. Continuously solving challenges reinforces their confidence and possibly their self-worth. When done repeatedly, it becomes part of who they believe they are. The reason this is difficult to stop is that, in some part, it means changing their identity.

By repeatedly saving the day and being told you’re the “glue that keeps everything together” and other such phrases disguised as compliments, you are introducing cognitive shortcuts. Leadership isn’t trying to trap you where you are, they are attempting to reduce uncertainty, and you’ve become a security blanket.

Stop Proving What Everyone Already Knows

Everyone already knows you are the competent one, there is no need to reinforce that reputation. Instead, start demonstrating competences they haven’t yet associated with you. Consider ways you can show them your strategic thinking, how well you influence others and get consensus, your ability to mentor future leaders, anticipate problems, and innovate.

People don’t promote what surprises them. They promote what they’ve already seen. They are scanning for repeatable and predictable patterns of certainty. If they’ve only seen you execute, that is what they will continuously reward.

Don’t Ask “How Can I Help?”

Before you automatically agree to help solve the next crisis or put out a fire you never started in the first place, ask yourself a few questions:

  • Who could use this opportunity as a stretch assignment to grow?
  • Where am I most valuable?
  • Is solving this problem the highest use of my expertise?
  • What problem can I prevent instead?
  • If I do solve this problem, who can I train in the process, so everyone doesn’t always rely on me?

While you might instinctively think you are being selfish by not jumping to solve the problem, what you are really exhibiting is leadership.

From Solving Problems to Creating Capacity

Instead of always being the temporary hero, consider how you can build systems that don’t require you to always be "on." Instead of being the expert, think about how you can develop experts, thereby creating a high-performing team. Instead of solving every issue yourself, you are creating opportunities for tomorrow. That is the transition that leaders are looking for when determining who should get a promotion.

The Competency Tax isn’t paid because you’re too talented. The check has been cashed because everyone, likely including you, has become comfortable with an expired definition of your value. Sure, competence gets you noticed, but if it becomes your entire identity, it can create a suffocating ceiling to your career.

The goal is never to become less dependable. It is simply to be known for something bigger than being the person who always is relied on to save the day.

item.title: The Origins of My Spirituality
item.description:
Identity

The Origins of My Spirituality

A Personal Perspective: Understanding myself through my narrative identity.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Is the spirituality the result of education and wisdom, or does it start early in life?
  • Narrative identity is defined as the internalized story we construct about ourselves.
  • Our deepest values and characteristic ways of making meaning appear early in our lives.
Source: ForGaby/Shutterstock

What is the origin of our spirituality? Is it the result of education and wisdom attained through years of schooling and life experiences, or does it start very early in life?

A patient’s mother once asked me how I became so spiritual. My initial response was that I learned from my patients, once I started using hypnosis and directly interacting with their subconscious.

But as I reflected on the question, and looked backward across my life, I found parts of the answer in fiction stories I wrote as a teenager, and in my experiences as a young child. My spirituality, it turns out, appears to have been there all along.

The Potionmaker

For instance, I remembered a story I wrote as an 18-year-old in which I explored reasons why a life of limited length may be better than immortality. In the story, the Potionmaker offers a potion of everlasting life to three individuals.

He tells the first one that before he decides whether to take the potion, he should know that the Potionmaker has proven that there is no existence after death. The Potionmaker is asked if he has taken the potion, and says that he has not. He explains that if life is everlasting, it is too long. Once a person accomplishes all his goals, he then must live an eternity of boredom.

He tells the second individual that he has proven that there is no way to tell if there is existence after death. The Potionmaker admits that he has not taken the potion because he does not want to miss out on the opportunity to exist in an afterlife.

He tells the third individual that he has proven with complete certainty that there is an existence after death. The individual agrees that the Potionmaker is correct and explains that this is why he wants the potion. Apparently, he has killed a man and knows where he will go once he dies. The Potionmaker agrees that this would be a good reason to take the potion.

The man drinks the potion quickly, and faces the doorway, away from the Potionmaker. The man says, “Will I live forever now?”

“Yes,” replied the Devil.

Escape from Death

At 17, I wrote a story about Harry Houdini, the famous escape artist, who promised that once he died, he would escape death and return to Earth. In my story, Houdini finally succeeds in escaping and returns triumphantly.

To his chagrin he discovers that in his absence the end of time already had arrived, and thus death no longer exists. This story touches upon the idea that sometimes achieving our goals can lead to an unexpected outcome that we may not even desire.

The Big Bang

At 15, I wrote a story about an astronaut who is exploring the edge of the universe. While he is doing so, the universe begins collapsing into a small singularity. The astronaut recognizes that once the universe collapses, it will be no more. Therefore, he crashes his spaceship into the tiny universe which kills him and causes the universe to explode in a Big Bang.

The story concludes with the first verses of the Bible: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Now the earth was a formless void and the spirit of God hovered over the water.” In this story, then, the referenced spirit could have been that of the astronaut, which thus raises the possibility that the creator of the universe is very different from what we believe about Him.

Respecting Life

At seven, when I still lived in Israel, I went with my mother to Tel Aviv. A man had caught some wild birds and was selling them for a Lira (Israeli currency at the time). I wanted to buy two birds with my allowance money, which my mother allowed me to do. Then, as I had planned, I set them free.

Finally, my mother told me that at five I wanted to fish. I was very excited when my father purchased a fishing pole for me and we went fishing for the first time. I even caught a fish on my first try. And immediately I wanted to throw it back into the water because it was only then that it dawned on me that the fish might die.

Both of these encounters demonstrate my respect for life as a child and this concern may have been at the core of my decision to become a physician.

So, from where did my spirituality come at such a young age? I suspect it’s the result of input from my subconscious.

Narrative Identity

Narrative identity has been defined as the internalized story we construct about our lives that provides life with some degree of unity and purpose (McAdams & McLean, 2013). Research suggests that our deepest values and characteristic ways of making meaning appear early and often remain consistent throughout our lifetime.

Looking back at my own stories, I can see exactly what this means. The questions I was asking as a teenager are the ones I am still exploring today including about the nature of death, the relationship between human action and creation, and how our deepest intentions and actions can lead to unexpected outcomes.

Takeaway

As we think about our life stories that we consider important we can develop better self-understanding.

item.title: Brothers, Sisters, and Divorce: What Happens Between the Kids
item.description:
Divorce

Brothers, Sisters, and Divorce: What Happens Between the Kids

Divorce reshapes sibling dynamics, bringing them closer or dividing them.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Divorce can bring siblings closer or create distance, shaping lifelong dynamics between them.
  • Sibling roles like protector, scapegoat, or caretaker often persist well into adulthood post-divorce.
  • Open conversations help adult siblings repair bonds and reframe childhood divorce roles together.

“I think our parents’ divorce brought my sister and me closer than ever. We got each other through those hard years,” Jonah told me. “She was my rock,” Jonah added. “Our parents weren’t very stable then, so we held on to each other instead. She was my protector.”

Another client, Frank, describes another common change in sibling dynamics. “My brother withdrew and shut down when I needed to lean on him. He turned to friends for support, and I felt lost without him. He grew more and more distant, and our relationship has never recovered.

Same event, opposite outcomes — this is what divorce does to the bond between siblings. While most divorce advice focuses on the parent-child relationship, siblings often become each other's most important attachment figures during the divorce.

How divorce reshapes sibling dynamics

When parents are overwhelmed by emotions, conflict, or the time-consuming logistics of divorce, siblings often turn to each other. The shared experience can bring siblings closer, or it can divide them, depending on each child’s temperament and often on how each child perceives the divorce.

Sometimes an older sibling assumes a caretaking role with the younger siblings, as my client, Jonah, experienced.

Sometimes children have very different relationships with each parent, which may lead to splits as they each align with the parent they feel needs their support.

Siblings who lived through the same divorce often describe it very differently, shaped by the age or stage they were at when it happened.

Sometimes children are separated in custody arrangements, which may also cause distance in the sibling relationship.

Common sibling patterns that emerge during and after divorce

The protector/protected dynamic: The protector sibling often manages the emotions of the other siblings and may become parentified.

Splitting along parental lines: Some children see one parent as more needy or fragile, and in need of help. Some children turn against the parent whom they see as the guilty parent, the one to blame. A child might see one parent as a victim and support them. Other children may align with the parent they can count on for care and security.

Scapegoating and/or favoritism: Sometimes a parent unconsciously blames or favors one child, which can lead to conflict, competition, or resentment between the siblings.

The "united front" bond: Some siblings become fiercely loyal to each other in the face of the feeling that the family is falling apart.

Divergent coping styles: Frank, whose brother withdrew rather than leaned in, is a good example. When one sibling internalizes or withdraws, another may begin to externalize or act out. This creates turmoil and drama in the family, which may distract the parents from the trauma of the divorce, and which can cause friction between the siblings.

How these patterns evolve after the divorce

Teen siblings may compete for stability or attention from an overwhelmed parent, may act out, or become depressed or anxious. Some teens look for alternate “family” elsewhere, through friend groups, other adults or mentors, or, in more troubling cases, other risky peer groups.

As siblings mature into young adulthood, their old roles often persist even after everyone's grown. Siblings may continue to enact the roles they assumed during the divorce for decades, as protector, scapegoat, loner, caretaker, etc.

Family gatherings, weddings, and holidays can reactivate childhood divorce-era roles. They may be reactivated as they marry, become parents, grandparents, and wounds can reopen if a sibling gets divorced.

Later in life, unresolved sibling dynamics from the divorce often resurface in decisions about caregiving of aging parents.

Why adult siblings sometimes drift apart

Siblings often have very different narratives about the family divorce, and see their parents very differently. This can lead them to different loyalties and create blind spots and distance.

Often a sibling will carry resentment about which sibling was favored, or "had it easier."

When one sibling is viewed as the family's healthy one and one still feels stuck, they can trigger each other and perpetuate the family dynamic.

What parents can do to protect siblings

Avoid assigning roles ("you're in charge of your brother now"). Don’t let a child become a messenger or “spy” on the other parent. Avoid inviting a child to be your confidante or “friend.” Never communicate that you are comparing your children.

Allow siblings to process the divorce with each other, not just individually with parents, while reassuring them that you are still able to be a strong, secure, safe parent.

Be alert to loyalty binds that may surface, and show your children that loyalty to one parent doesn't require distancing from a sibling loyal to the other.

What adult siblings can do to repair or strengthen the bond

If you and your siblings would like to repair your relationships, start by talking about and naming the roles you each played as kids. Listen to each other’s versions of the divorce with curiosity and open-mindedness, and without blame. Recognize that you each probably had different relationships to the same parents.

Sibling relationships are often the longest relationships people have in life — longer than the marriage that ended, and often longer than the relationship with either parent. Divorce can strengthen the sibling relationship, or it can fracture it. But it is never too late to repair that relationship, and often a family therapist can facilitate the conversation and the healing of old wounds.

My client, Frank, invited his brother to join him for a few sessions to try to build a stronger relationship. It was the first time they talked about their childhoods and their parents’ divorce. As they shared their experiences, the wall between them began to come down. The last time I saw them, they were planning a camping trip with their children.
